title: Class 10: Aggregate Demand/Supply and Macroeconomic Policy
coverageSummary: The AD-AS model as a joint analysis of output and inflation fluctuations in the short and long run; long-run equilibrium (actual output = potential output, actual inflation = expected inflation) versus temporary short-run equilibrium; the downward-sloping AD curve, with the monetary policy reaction function (MPRF, r = r* + g(pi - pi*)) as its main slope explanation alongside wealth, distributional, uncertainty, and international effects; the distinction between a movement along AD (a change in r for a given MPRF) and a shift of AD (a change in the MPRF itself, a demand shock, or stabilization policy); the AS curve's short-run equation (Y = h(P - expected P) + potential output), inflation inertia (driven by inflation expectations and long-term contracts), and the three causes of an AS shift (resources/technology, inflation expectations, and inflation shocks such as the 1973 oil shock); the output-gap/inflation-direction relationship; the self-correcting economy and the speed-of-adjustment tradeoff for stabilization policy; how the economy responds to an inflation shock under a 'do-nothing' MPRF versus an 'accommodating' policy response that resets the long-run inflation target higher; shocks to potential output ('capacity shocks'); the 1970s-80s Great Inflation and Volcker's disinflationary recession; the post-1980s Great Moderation in output and inflation volatility; central-bank credibility and its determinants (independence, reputation, explicit inflation targets); the political backlash against the 2008-09 policy response and the broader macroeconomic lessons drawn from that crisis; and policy lags (the inside lag and the outside lag, and how monetary versus fiscal policy compare on each).
reliabilityNotes: 35 slides' bullet text and speaker notes extracted cleanly via python-pptx, including the AS equation and Fed policy-response speaker notes on slides 16 and 21. Slides 25-29 and 32 (an oil-price chart, a Volcker-recession chart, two further photo/chart-only slides, a real-GDP-volatility chart, and an 'Inflation Targeting' chart) are diagram/photo-only with no extractable body text; their underlying narrative is fully carried by the surrounding slides' bullet text (24, 30, 31), so no question depends on reading these charts' pixels. No question in this source's set required a needsReview flag.

title: Economics Focus: Much Ado About Multipliers (The Economist, 2009)
coverageSummary: Why economists disagree about the size of the fiscal multiplier: the definition of the multiplier and why it should be near zero at full capacity but can exceed one in a recession; how the multiplier varies by the type of fiscal action (spending versus tax cuts, and by who receives a tax cut); how crowding-out (higher interest rates reducing private investment) and crowding-in (higher confidence raising private investment) affect the multiplier's size; Ricardian-equivalence-style concerns about future tax expectations reducing the multiplier; the difficulty of empirically isolating fiscal policy's effect from the business cycle itself; and why post-war multiplier estimates (often based on military spending) may not transfer cleanly to the 2008-09 stimulus (near-zero interest rates, more credit-constrained consumers, more indebted governments).

title: Lessons from the Great Depression for Policy Today (Christina Romer, 2013 speech transcript)
coverageSummary: Three policy lessons drawn from the Great Depression recovery (starting 1933) and compared to the 2008-09 crisis response: (1) fiscal policy 'works when it is tried' -- the 1933-34 Civil Works Administration and 1936 veterans' bonus show expansionary fiscal policy helped, while the 1937 fiscal contraction preceded the 1937-38 recession, paralleling the 2009 Recovery Act (helpful, but likely too small) and 2010s austerity debates; (2) at the zero lower bound, monetary policy 'takes a regime shift' -- Roosevelt's 1933 exit from the gold standard changed deflation expectations to mild-inflation expectations even at a zero nominal rate, a lesson only partially followed by the Fed's post-2008 quantitative easing and forward guidance (contrasted with Japan's 'Abenomics' regime shift); and (3) credit policy should 'get debt burdens down quickly' -- the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's mortgage principal write-downs in the 1930s versus the slower, more limited mortgage-renegotiation response after 2008.
reliabilityNotes: Clean pdftotext -layout extraction of a full speech transcript (1219 lines), read in full through the conclusion. Per the 'prioritize core arguments over exhaustive coverage' rule for long readings, this bank's questions focus on the three headline policy lessons (fiscal, monetary, credit) and their explicit 1930s-vs-2008 comparisons rather than every historical anecdote in the transcript (e.g., detailed veterans'-bonus survey evidence, the Martha Olney car-loan-forfeiture study). This is a released academic/public speech transcript with citations, not an exam or answer key, so no academic-integrity concern applies. No question in this source's set required a needsReview flag.
